pr_title: Extend settings_runtime_commit to support all commits
pr_body:
This replaces settings_runtime_commit() with a wrapper for settings_commit_subtree(), extending the functionality to support global commit and nested subtree commits.

Fixes #51703
pr_comments: Please also add commit with release notes entry mentioning the Zephyr issue being fixed.

issue_context.title: settings_runtime_commit lacks global and full subtree commit
issue_context.body:
settings_runtime_commit() is quite limited in functionality, and completely redundant with settings_commit_subtree()

- does not handle global commit of all settings.
- does not implement DYNAMIC settings

Suggested action is to replace it's implementation with just a call to settings_commit_subtree() which implements the full functionality needed on settings commit.
comments: @hno-addiva thanks for the report. Would you be willing to open a Pull Request with your suggested fix?
You are too fast. Already working on it.
Just realised the bug is smaller than I thought. It does support DYNAMIC settings. But not global or even subtree commits (all handlers below a node), only explicit node commits.

> @carlescufi should we port this to 3.2?

No, let's get the PR merged first and then we'll see.

review_comments:
TBH I don't know what should be the use case and how should the `settings_runtime_commit()` work. It was introduced in 94451b22fcc6a068de2a2982b202772c6bbefae8, but there is no specific reason **why** it was added. At least that is not clear to me.

Why don't you use `settings_commit_subtree()` directly, if that is what you expect?

I have no opinion either way. I also thought of proposing it to be dropped as useless. Having a settings_runtime_commit() makes the runtime settings API complete, but at the same time is quite redundant with settings_commit() and settings_commit_subtree().

The existing settings_runtime_commit() implementation is odd and not very useful imho, more like a handler debug API call than actual useful API call and as such belongs more in settings as settings_call_commit_handler() or the like than in settings_runtime. Very unexpected that child nodes do not get commited, easily causing inconsistent runtime results when only an upper node is committed and not it's child nodes. And also lacking a global commit.

But not going to work more on this at the moment. The project where we was using Zephyr is unfortunately on hold (but not due to Zephyr fault). We will surely come back to Zephyr in future.

I also question the validity of the test case. Silently accepting commit of a non-existing sub-tree in a call that can only commit a single explicit settings node? Additionally, there is no test of settings_commit_subtree().

> I also thought of proposing it to be dropped as useless.

I was not using `settings_runtime` recently and actually this was my first view into `settings_runtime_commit()` implementation. But my first impression was that it should be dropped.

This is also the reason why I referenced 94451b22fcc6a068de2a2982b202772c6bbefae8, which provides no explanation why it was introduced in the first place. And from that commit we can see that the only user of this API were some test cases.

Just sharing my concerns here, I don't have strong opinion on that. I think also that we lack some sort of guidelines for when to use settings vs settings_runtime and what should be the use cases. At least that is not clear to me, even after using both, I am still not certain that I am doing it in a valid way.

My understanding (and demonstrated in working code, and works out very well) is that there is two primary ways of modifying settings via API.

a) settings_save_one() for each settings that should change, followed by reloading the settings (in whole, or individual subtree) to activate the new settings (also calls commit)

b) settings_runtime_set() followed by commit to activate settings runtime. And then at a later time settings_save() once verified working to make the settings to be stored in persistent storage.

settings_runtime_get/set accesses the owners (code/application) version of the settings (via the get/set methods of the settings node), and can also access settings that have no automatic persistent storage mapping (not serialised to storage on settings_save()).

The code/application can also directly modify it's settings internally directly in it's variables, which will get exported to persistent store on settings_save().

The middle ground is also possible, testing settings runtime via settings_runtime_set()+commit, and then saving them persistent with settings_save_one(). Works reasonably well. But can become confusing if a modified setting is not already saved in backing store as a reload of the settings will then keep the runtime setting until reboot and it may go unnoticed that the setting haven't been made persistent. There is no concept of "default settings" when reloading the settings, it always loads any persistent settings ontop of what is currently running.

My preferred method is settings_save_one() followed by reload when all settings that should change have been done.

But the settings_runtime_get/set/commit API is also very nice for testing things out without making them persistent, and to expose debug settings/parameters.

Have not really bothered with settings_save(). Risks saving too much settings. Better to keep unmodified settings at their "application default", and let them update when the application is updated. But that's my preference. Others may prefer to have the full settings configuration saved. In our application we had many detail settings that is irrelevant for most configurations.
